title: The Evidence Behind The Will to Learn
author: Stuart Jr., Dave
summary: Responding to a California teacher’s request for research to argue the student motivation case with district leaders, Stuart marshals two comprehensive bodies of evidence: John Hattie’s Visible Learning meta-analysis (130,000 studies, 400+ million students) and Camille Farrington et al.’s critical literature review Teaching Adolescents to Become Learners. He grounds the discussion first in practical data from Grand River Prep HS, which saw SAT scores surpass the state average and AP pass rates improve after one year of intentional Five Key Beliefs implementation. He then maps specific Hattie effect sizes to Will to Learn strategies—Teacher Credibility (1.09), Student Expectations (1.23), Collective Efficacy (1.34)—before detailing the Farrington report’s research base for each of the four academic mindsets. The article is the most comprehensive single-document case Stuart has made for the research authority behind his motivational framework, written to be cited directly in professional advocacy conversations.
points: Hattie’s Visible Learning reveals that factors central to the Five Key Beliefs—Teacher Credibility (1.09 effect size), Student Expectations (1.23), Collective Efficacy (1.34), Teaching Students to Drive Their Learning (0.96)—rank among the most powerful influences on student outcomes in the largest educational meta-analysis ever conducted.

The problem with how schools apply Visible Learning is cherry-picking isolated high-effect factors; The Will to Learn is designed as a coherent system for leveraging several of those factors simultaneously in a teacher-accessible framework.

The Farrington et al. literature review identified the four academic mindsets (Value, Effort, Efficacy, Belonging) as a cluster strongly influencing academic perseverance, with specific study citations: Hulleman-Harackiewicz found 0.80 GPA improvements from utility-value writing; Walton-Cohen found 52% reduction in the racial achievement gap through a belonging intervention.

Grand River Prep HS data—SAT scores surpassing the state average and rising AP pass rates after one year of targeted Five Key Beliefs implementation—provides real-world evidence that the framework produces measurable institutional outcomes.

Student motivation is not a feel-good supplement to rigorous instruction; it is, in Hattie’s framework, foundational to virtually every factor that drives student outcomes and must be addressed with frequency, intentionality, and intelligence.
quotes: The only thing wrong with John Hattie’s career-long, herculean meta-analysis is that it’s too good. Visible Learning is way too good. It represents the largest scale analysis of educational research ever conducted — insanely large, as in 130,000 studies are represented in it, involving more than 400,000,000 students from around the world.

The Will to Learn is basically a book that asks, ‘What if you came up with an approach to leveraging some of the most powerful things in Visible Learning and framed it in accessible, teacher-friendly language — by a practicing teacher, for practicing teachers?
Teacher Credibility = 1.09 effect size. This one’s a whopper. And that’s one of the reasons it’s the base of the Five Key Beliefs pyramid.

All of my work has a beguiling simplicity to it. It’s so simple that it appears dumb. “We already do this,” I hear folks say. And to this I agree — many of us do do the things I recommend in The Will to Learn. The problem I’m trying to remedy is that we don’t do the things I describe in the book with the frequency and intentionality and awareness and intelligence that they merit.

Research by Hulleman and Harackiewicz (2009) found that students who wrote about how science topics applied to their lives saw 0.80 grade point improvements — demonstrating the power of value cultivation.

Walton and Cohen’s (2011) belonging interventions with African American college students resulted in 0.24 grade point improvements sustained through senior year and reduced the racial achievement gap by 52%.
Student motivation is NOT just a feel-good topic. It’s NOT a thing to touch on and move ahead to fancier things. It is fundamental.
